creator: nataindata
caption:
I’d end up rich according to Monte Carlo simulation

Monte Carlo simulation is a technique that runs thousands (or millions) of “what if” scenarios to predict possible outcomes when there’s uncertainty involved.

🇲🇨 Named after the famous casino city in Monaco, it uses randomness to model real-world unpredictability.

🤑 How it helps predict wealth:

When it comes to personal finance or investments, Monte Carlo simulations can:

• Model different market conditions (bull runs, crashes, sideways markets)
• Account for variables like inflation, salary changes, and spending habits
• Show you the probability of reaching your financial goals
• Stress-test your retirement plan against worst-case scenarios
 
🔮 Instead of saying “you’ll have $1M at 65,” it tells you “there’s an 85% chance you’ll have between $800K and $1.5M.”

So yes, technically Monte Carlo told me I’d be rich. 
It just didn’t mention which simulation run that was

creator: algobrief
caption:
Interesting fact:

When you press Ctrl+C in a terminal, your shell sends a SIGINT (Signal Interrupt, signal #2) to the foreground process group — not just the process itself. The process can actually catch or ignore SIGINT using signal handlers, which is why some programs like vim or custom scripts don't immediately die when you press it. For a guaranteed kill, you'd escalate to SIGKILL (signal #9) via kill -9 <PID>, which cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored by any process.

Have you ever had Ctrl+C fail on you mid-script — and did you know why?

creator: pdavisjones
caption:
Samethink & the Strait

The wall-to-wall coverage of the Strait of Hormuz has been consistent: it’s closed, and the world is on the brink of catastrophe.

But what does “closed” actually mean?

Because on the ground, the reality looks very different.

A research group sent someone directly into the region—through Oman, onto a locally piloted boat—to see it firsthand. What he found was not an empty strait. It was active. Ships are moving. In some cases, they’re even rerouting—but they’re still getting through. Notably, a number of Chinese vessels continue to pass.

So why does the global narrative lack this nuance?

Because much of modern reporting relies on a single system: AIS (Automatic Identification System) data. And here’s the problem: there’s an entire “shadow fleet” of ships that either go dark or spoof their locations. Thousands of vessels operating outside that visibility.

So if your lens is AIS… you’re only seeing part of the picture.

And this points to something bigger.

In the name of efficiency, we’re increasingly outsourcing our understanding of the world to single data sources, centralized narratives, and now, even AI systems.

But truth is often less efficient.

It requires friction. It requires verification. Sometimes, it requires going there yourself.

That’s the difference between consuming information… and actually understanding reality.
#news #politics #iran #ai
transcript: There's a crazy story about this research company who sent a guy literally to the Strait of Hormuz, and he found out that the situation wasn't at all way that we are reading in the media. And it made me think about how in a drive for efficiency, we have a collapsing diversity of thought. The backstory is of course here that we're all reading about the Strait of Hormuz being closed, how it's a crisis, and how no one, not even Beijing, is getting through the Strait of Hormuz. But this research outfit that runs a substack hired analyst number three who's fluid in four language and sent him with a box of Cuban cigars, 15 grand in cash, and a role of zen. Literally this briefcase, two Oman, which is right here. He crossed into Oman and promised not to engage in journalism of any kind, but in his briefcase he had a microphone kit and recording sunglasses. He hires a stranger to take him on a boat out into the Strait of Hormuz. And he finds that there's actually a lot of activity going on there. He calls it manage chaos, there weren't any mines, and there was lots of traffic, especially Chinese vessels, and that they were using alternate routes that nobody was talking about. It turns out that the reason that we get all these same type of reports out of mainstream media outlets, is that in their drive for efficiency, they all use this automatic identification or AIS data, which is basically shipping data that is published to this website. And it tells you where ships are, but the thing is that Iran and China they often use these shadow fleet vessels that are these unmarked vessels that even paint the tops of their holes so that satellites can't identify them. And they specifically spoof their location to manipulate the AIS data. So all these guys are looking at the same wrong data. And I understand that when politicians are talking about reopening the Strait of Hormuz, they're talking about free travel of vessels, not the shadow fleet. But analyst number three and his Hormuz field trip showed us that by actually going there and seeing for themselves, there's a lot more to the story. And it made me think about a conversation I had with a very smart, way smarter than me, billionaire investor, not too long ago, where he said, be careful about relying on AI systems to help you with creativity. Because they can be sort of single points of data, just like this AIS data. It leads everyone to the same outcomes. Because if you see here, humans are the light colored dots. They kind of think about a topic all over the place. But AI systems, they're these filled in dots. They tend to always cluster around the same thoughts because they're computers. So what we're seeing is that there is a collapsing diversity of thought because in a drive for efficiency, so many people are using AI systems to guide their thinking. When sometimes the inefficient thing of taking a field trip out into the place, which is not that efficient, can actually tell you what's going on. Do you see examples of companies and individuals starting to think the same because they're using single sources of data that are often wrong or don't tell the whole story? Genuine question, do we have a collapsing diversity of thought and analysis?

creator: elfisicobarbudo
caption: #fisica #ciencia #curiosidades #shrek #sabiasque
transcript: Seguro que no sabías que si abres una imagen en Photoshop, la desenfocas, la enfocas y repite ese proceso una y otra vez acabas con esto. Y entiendo que ahora esté flipando pepinillos, eso es un patrón de Turin. Los patrones de Turin son aquellos que podemos encontrar en el animal print, como las manchas de un leopardo o las rayas de una cebra. Pero ¿qué tiene que ver a él enfocar y desenfocar con estos patrones complejos? La respuesta nos lleva a principios de los años 50, cuando Alan Turin propuso una teoría revolucionaria sobre cómo se forman los patrones en la naturaleza. Tenemos dos sustancias químicas interactuando, un activador que puede estimular en la producción de melarina, que da el color a la piel y un inhibidor, que bloquea el activador. En Photoshop el desenfocca actúa como un inhibidor, prohibizando dispersando la información, mientras que el enfocca juega el rol del activador, acentuando contrastes y bordes. Al repetir estos pasos, creamos una reacción química digital, una competencia entre homogenizar la imagen y crear contrastes locales. Aunque estamos trabajando con píxeles y frutos digitales, el resultado se semeja a los patrones que vemos en la naturaleza y que apareceré en lo que más mola de un universo, los animales y la intro de Dan and Dan. La escala y el tipo de patrones que aparecen dependen de cómo ajustemos los radios de desenfocca y el enfoque, y así puedes crearte tus fondos de pantalla con texturas chulas y mensajes ocultos.
